scenes.vo: Two giant black holes, shining side by side, just nine hundred million years after the Big Bang.
scenes.cap: Two giant black holes, side by side, 900 million years after the Big Bang

scenes.vo: The James Webb Space Telescope found the oldest pair of black hole powered quasars ever seen.
scenes.cap: JWST: the oldest pair of black hole-powered quasars ever seen

scenes.vo: We see them as they were when the universe was only a thirteenth of its age.
scenes.cap: Seen when the universe was just 1/13 of its age

scenes.vo: They are just eighteen thousand one hundred light years apart. About one fifth the width of our Milky Way.
scenes.cap: Only 18,100 light-years apart: about 1/5 of the Milky Way's width

scenes.vo: One black hole weighs one point five billion Suns. The other, four hundred million.
scenes.cap: Masses: 1.5 billion Suns and 400 million Suns

scenes.vo: The lead author says there's no definitive theoretical explanation for how a pair like this existed so early.
scenes.cap: Lead author: "no definitive theoretical explanation" yet

scenes.vo: Nine hundred million years old, and already this huge. So how did they grow so fast?
scenes.cap: Published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters, 10 Nov 2026
